notes.meaning: Parents are told to answer their children by explaining how God passed over their houses when He brought judgment on Egypt. Hearing this, the people bowed their heads in humble worship before the rescue had even taken place. Remembering God's past mercy gives believers confidence for the future.

The Israelites went and carefully followed every instruction they had received from Moses and Aaron. Their safety depended on putting the blood on the doorposts as God had commanded, not just believing the promise in their minds. True trust in God always shows itself in action.

At midnight, the darkest and quietest hour, the Lord struck down every firstborn male in Egypt. The judgment reached everyone from Pharaoh's heir on the throne to the lowliest prisoner in the dungeon. No human status or power could protect anyone from God's righteous sentence.

Pharaoh and all the Egyptians woke up in the night to find that someone had died in nearly every home. Loud wailing filled the whole country as families discovered their loss. The sudden grief finally broke Egypt's stubborn refusal to let God's people go.

Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron in the middle of the night and commanded the Israelites to leave immediately. He gave up every condition he had fought for, telling them to take all their families and animals. Crushed by sorrow and fear, he even asked Moses to pray for a blessing on him.

The Egyptian people pleaded with the Israelites to leave their land as quickly as possible. They were terrified that if the Israelites stayed any longer, everyone in Egypt would die. Fear drove them to speed up the departure of the people they had enslaved.

Because the Egyptians pushed them to leave immediately, the people could not wait for their dough to rise. They bundled their shallow wooden bread bowls into their cloaks and carried them on their shoulders. God used this sudden rush to start their seven-day feast of bread made without yeast.

The Israelites obeyed Moses by asking their Egyptian neighbors for silver, gold, and fine clothing. God made the Egyptians willing to hand over their treasures, so Israel left with great riches. This was not stealing, but fair payment for years of unpaid slave labor.

The Israelites set out from Rameses and marched toward Succoth, their first campsite. There were roughly six hundred thousand fighting men on foot, not counting women and children. That meant the entire company moving together numbered around two million people.

A large crowd of non-Israelite foreigners journeyed out of Egypt alongside the Israelites. Many of these people were drawn by the great wonders God had performed, while others simply wanted to escape a ruined country. They also brought vast herds of sheep, goats, and cattle with them.

The people baked flat bread from the unrisen dough they had carried out of Egypt. They had been driven out so fast that they could not pack regular supplies or wait for yeast to work. What began as a hurried flight became a lasting symbol of how God swiftly rescued them.

The Israelites had lived as wanderers and slaves for exactly four hundred and thirty years since God's original promise to Abraham. On that exact anniversary, the entire nation marched out like an organized army under the Lord's direction. God always keeps His promises right on schedule.

The Lord stayed on watch all through that night to lead His people safely out of Egyptian bondage. Because God kept this vigil, the Israelites were instructed to stay awake and celebrate this night for all generations to come. Believers are called to keep God's past rescues fresh in their memories.

God gave Moses and Aaron specific rules about who could take part in the Passover meal. Foreigners who did not belong to the covenant community were not allowed to eat it. The meal was reserved for those who had committed themselves to the God of Israel.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary sees the Passover as a picture of Holy Communion, which is reserved only for baptized believers in full fellowship with the Church.

notes.meaning: Any slave purchased with money was permitted to eat the Passover after being circumcised. Circumcision was a physical sign that brought a person into God's covenant family. This law gave servants full spiritual standing in the religious life of the home.

Visitors staying temporarily and paid day laborers were excluded from eating the Passover. Since they were not permanent members of the covenant household, they could not join in its sacred meal. God's special meal was meant only for those fully committed to His family.

The entire Passover lamb had to be eaten inside one house, and none of the meat could be taken outside. In addition, none of its bones could be broken, which kept the family eating together in haste. This command also pointed ahead to Jesus, the true Passover Lamb, whose bones were not broken on the cross.

The whole community of Israel was commanded to celebrate the Passover. No one in the covenant was allowed to neglect this feast of thanksgiving. Sharing in God's great salvation brought a joyful duty to thank Him together.

Any foreigner living in the land who wanted to keep the Passover had to circumcise every male in his household first. Once that covenant mark was received, he was treated with the exact same spiritual rights as a native-born Israelite. God opened the door for people from other nations to join His people under one shared law.

All the people of Israel did exactly what the Lord had ordered through Moses and Aaron. Their united obedience prepared them to step out of slavery and into freedom. When God's people trust and obey His directions, He works powerfully on their behalf.

On that very day, the Lord brought the people of Israel out of Egypt in orderly companies. Rather than running in confusion, they marched out like an organized army led by God Himself. God proved Himself completely true to the promise He had made to deliver them.
